utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to say a few words about the nexus between the alleged existence of an international armed conflict and the crimes from Article 2 of the Statute. In our submission, the Prosecution failed to prove the existence of this nexus. Instead of explaining the nexus between the crimes and the international armed conflict, the Prosecution simplified things and just say that General Praljak was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and seems to consider that fact to be sufficient. An explanation is missing, and so is concrete evidence to show that there undoubtedly is a nexus between the crimes from Article 2 of the Statute and the international armed conflict. The mere presence of General Praljak in Bosnia-Herzegovina is not sufficient grounds for such a conclusion. Concerning the Prosecution's allegation in paragraph 78 of their final brief, in other words, the mens rea in connection with the international armed conflict, I would like to say the following: The Prosecution claimed that all the accused were fully aware of the intensive involvement of the Republic of Croatia in the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They base this claim on alleged regular contacts with the relevant bodies or persons in the Republic of Croatia, and go on to claim that the intervention of Croatia was so intensive in the period in question that it would be impossible to believe that the accused were unaware of the existence of links and the involvement of the Republic of Croatia in the Croatian-Muslim conflict. So the only thesis is indirect conclusions, they can't have failed -- they can't have failed to do this and that. It is true that Croatia was involved in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it was involved in the war in which the aggressor, the JNA, waged against Bosnia-Herzegovina and in which the HVO, and later the BH Army, opposed this aggression, but not with the intention to help one party to that conflict. The Republic of Croatia is a necessary participant in this war, but not a willing participant. There is no safety for the Republic of Croatia as long as the un-safety in Bosnia-Herzegovina exists because their mutual border is over 1.000 kilometres long. There is no safety for Croatia while the JNA, or the Serbs, are attacking Bosnia-Herzegovina but, simultaneously, they're also attacking Croatia with the same plan, to conquer territories in both countries regardless of the border between them. There is no safety for Croatia while it is a point of transit for the supply of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in general, for the supply of humanitarian aid, and while 300.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina are present in Croatia, to leave it at that. All that shows that the Republic of Croatia is a necessary participant in that war, but it isn't involved in the war of its own will. The Republic of Croatia is a subject and a victim in that war, if it wishes that were not. It's not a result of will or the policy of Croatia, it's a result of the acts of others; specifically, the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbs, which is beyond the control of Croatia. The Republic of Croatia thus had a legitimate interest in the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was its duty to take measures to prevent chaos, measures to put up a defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and co-operation with the HVO to be able to defend its own territory; first of all, the southern front, but also the Croatian Posavina, Slavonski Brod, and other areas that were directly threatened or attacked from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can refer to the testimony of General Praljak and that of General Petkovic. In the case of General Petkovic, the transcript page is 49702 through 49704. The date is 18 February 2010. In Praljak's case, the motives are even more obvious than in Petkovic's, but many other people, just like General Praljak, also went to Bosnia-Herzegovina to defend their native area. It's a relevant question, whether Croatia had the intention to help one party in one of the additional conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina; specifically, the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, which came about as a consequence of the aggression of the JNA. That was a conflict that nobody planned or foresaw except, probably -- this is speculation now -- except probably the JNA, which contributed to that conflict to weaken the resistance that the BH Army and the HVO put up to prevent it from achieving its objectives. There is no evidence to indicate that General Praljak or any other accused were in a position to know or foresee what the Republic of Croatia, or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or the VRS, or the international community, or anybody would do in the days or weeks to come. All these I mentioned were players there, and nobody could know what any of these players would do on the following day. The Prosecution implicitly claims that General Praljak was so much smarter than anybody else that he could know with certainty and he could foresee future events which, by the way, nobody foresaw. As for the awareness of the participants of the alleged international armed conflict, the Defence reiterates that throughout the conflicts -- sorry, throughout the alleged conflict or throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina in general, not one party, especially the representative Bosnia-Herzegovina, never once publicly and unambiguously stated that they see the other side, that is, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an enemy, or not even as a rival. So there were no two enemy countries, which is certainly a precondition for the existence of an international armed conflict. The political representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, and we have dealt with this extensively, had their own positions which sometimes were not harmonised, but, simultaneously, they participated in peace talks, patiently and very long, to find acceptable solutions, and it was Croatia which was the first to sign any solution that was offered, any plan. About the Prosecution's claim that the accused certainly knew and understood that Croatia was intensively involved in the conflict in BiH, among others, because there were regular contacts with the relevant bodies and persons in the Republic of Croatia, that is, based on the fact that there were such contacts with bodies and persons in Croatia, the Defence thinks it necessary to point out this information: The president of BiH, Alija Izetbegovic, was President Tudjman's guest more often than all these accused together, if they had a chance to ever meet President Tudjman. We made this analysis based on all presidential transcripts, both those that were admitted here and those that weren't, and the result is always the same. Then we may draw the same conclusion with regard to President Izetbegovic. He must have known what was going on. He was with Tudjman all the time. So this Prosecution claim certainly does not take us to the desired conclusion. The Defence wishes to show by this that the mere existence of contacts with Croatian officials is not sufficient ground for the conclusion that there was a single-mindedness about something only because there were contacts. With regard to the claim that there was mens rea in General Praljak with regard to the international armed conflict or, to quote paragraph 78 of their final brief, "his awareness of the involvement of Croatia in the conflict in BiH." [In English] The Prosecution has not made concrete efforts to specifically contradict Praljak's assertions and the assertions of the Praljak Defence. Regarding his motive to defend the people and state of the BiH, the Prosecution does not point to the various quotes from Praljak about his presence in BiH, the Banovina, et cetera, but it does not actually make the argument that Praljak was not there to defend against the Serbs, as the Defence asserted. We want to pose the following question to the Bench: What does it mean if our assertions with respect to Praljak's motive are correct? What does it mean if Praljak was there to defend BiH and her people? The answer should ultimately be, if our assertions are true, then this honourable Chamber cannot find proof of the requisite mens rea beyond a reasonable doubt. Then we should ask: Has the Prosecution proven that Praljak did not wish to defend BiH and her people? Was there no threat? Did the JNA aggression not exist ? Does the Prosecution deny the role of the JNA/VRS? Did Praljak lack a connection to BiH? Was he not born there? Did his family not living there? Finally, we should ask: If there are any doubt that had the HVO not been organised, the JNA would have killed and victimised countless more BiH citizens? Does this not demonstrate the motivation of Praljak and others like him more concretely than twisted interpretations, cherry-picked evidence? In the very last section of the Prosecution's oral argument last week, the Prosecution asked the honourable Trial Chamber to render a judgement that would sanction the war, generally, in the judgement that would somehow prevent future wars. At the heart of modern International Humanitarian Law is the principle of autonomy between questions of jus in bello and jus ad bellum. One aspect of that autonomy is that even if you do not agree with the reasons a party participated in a conflict, that does not change the criteria needed to prove a jus in bello violation. To the Prosecution, every casualty is inculpatory. The Prosecution, throughout the indictment, the trial, their final brief and closing argument, refers to the killing and wounding of Bosnian Muslims as though those tragedies were inherently criminal. Very frequently, no evidence is given as to the combat status of the casualties. The only possible deduction that can be made from this approach is that, to the Prosecution, the principle of autonomy does not apply. By effectively claiming that all tragedies are crimes, that all aid to the HVO was criminal, the Prosecution seeks to functionally destroy the principle of autonomy through pushing JCE theory to its outer-most extremes. Even if the Prosecution alleges the HVO was somehow a bad actor with respect to participating in a conflict, which would be a question of jus ad bellum, the Prosecution must still prove specifically every element of alleged violations of jus in bello. Unless the Prosecution could prove that the casualty was connected to a crime, not just the tragedy of war, then the fact of that casualty never should have been included in the indictment, and evidence on those casualties should never have been led. As Your Honours review the evidence, any evidence that shows the ills of war, rather than a crime, must be pointedly disregarded, lest the Trial Chamber be seen to follow the Prosecution's lead in disregarding the principle of autonomy between jus ad bellum and jus in bello. Such disregard is not only contrary to law, it is extremely dangerous, striking at the heart of the modern system of International Humanitarian Law. Just a moment, Your Honour. Your Honour, because of the time, I will skip now one subject which I planned to raise. Okay, then I will not, sorry. I will not, because it will be difficult to cover -- to cover all the details. [Interpretation] Greater Croatia: The Prosecution develops a thesis about an alleged plan of the Republic of Croatia to create a Greater Croatia within its historical borders, and essentially uses this thesis to explain the alleged motives and political plans of the Republic of Croatia, on which then, logically, a conclusion about the existence of a joint criminal enterprise can be based, as well as in the context of an international armed conflict. Thus, the Prosecution, in paragraphs 164 through 167, presents the political discussions of the president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, which, according to the Prosecution, show the existence of political and territorial claims of Croatia against the BiH. It's interesting to note immediately that in these paragraphs, the Prosecutor refers to the discussions of the Croatian political leaders that were held on the 8th of June, 1991, and the 27th of December, 1991, which is significantly earlier than the moment at which Bosnia-Herzegovina became a sovereign state, or just to be aware of the period, at the time when the break-up of the previous joint state of Yugoslavia began. This argument of the Prosecution is obviously irrelevant. Namely, these were the talks which President Tudjman had with his close associates at the time when the SFRY was breaking up, and neither the Republic of Croatia nor Bosnia-Herzegovina were, as yet, independent states. The SFRY was still in existence. So were the republics, the future independent states. All possible scenarios and options were considered. To provide the context of the thesis, I recall that the JNA, together with the local Serbs, occupied almost one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia in late 1991, and the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina had not broken out as yet, although it was quite certain that it would. The Prosecution simply ignores the fact that what follow after such discussions or thoughts which politicians expressed out loud, were specific actions. Thus, after such talks in March 1992, Tudjman and the HDZ took some specific steps to stimulate the Croats in the BiH to cast their votes at the referendum on the independence of BiH and to vote in favour of independence, that is to say, the creation of the new state of BiH, which I already mentioned. Therefore, considering possible political options or moves of the Republic of Croatia at this stage - that was the stage of the break-up of the Yugoslavia - resulted in the position that a contribution ought to be made to the creation of the new and independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is a fact. Considering political options or the possibilities which are at the disposal of a republic in relation to the federal Republic of Yugoslavia and other republics, under the circumstances of the break-up of the SFRY, is not just a legitimate right of the political leadership of a country, but also their duty; namely, to ascertain all the existing options and to select the one which is in the interest of this country. After the independent BiH was declared, there was not a single occasion on which the Croatian political leadership considered any options that would include a break-up of BiH or a change of the exterior borders of the BiH. Quite the contrary, when Izetbegovic offered to Tudjman to annex a part of the BiH territory, Tudjman refused that because he knew that this was not a solution, considering a series of new circumstances. The political leadership of the Republic of Croatia discussed a peaceful resolution to the war in BiH, which is, of course, quite legitimate because the BiH is a neighbouring country, and the Republic of Croatia cannot have any security without a stable Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the talks which were conducted at the time after the referendum, what was discussed was an internal division or internal configuration of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the various forms of a possible confederate Bosnia-Herzegovina or cantons, as we've often heard. Such initiatives also came from international mediators. The proposals for such a solution within Bosnia-Herzegovina were included in all peace plans, from the so-called Cutileiro Plan, to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and to the Dayton Accords, which eventually did include one such solution. However, the Prosecution interprets such discussions, which can be found in various presidential transcripts that we have seen during the trial, as something that demonstrates the intention of the Republic of Croatia to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a thesis, and other options are simply not considered. However, this interpretation is completely wrong, because this division has to do only with the modus of the internal configuration and system of government within Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why was the Republic of Croatia actively involved in this issue? It was not just the political interest of the Republic of Croatia, considering its security, as I already noted. There was also the insistence on part of the Western countries that the Republic of Croatia, that is to say, President Tudjman, by his personal authority which he enjoyed among the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, should influence them to accept the Western countries' proposed solutions or ideas, should the president of the Republic of Croatia have refused the requests of international officials and let the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina develop without any attempt to find solutions acceptable to the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In paragraphs 177 through 206, the Prosecution presents arguments about the presence of the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In spite of an extremely creative interpretation of evidence, the Prosecution has not managed to indicate a single direct piece of evidence which would undoubtedly demonstrate that a particular unit of the Croatian Army was present in Bosnia-Herzegovina and engaged in combat with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Prosecution has not presented such evidence, simply because such evidence does not exist, because this never happened. The Prosecution completely disregards the fact that the HVO was a component of the defence forces of BiH. The Prosecutor also completely disregards the fact that there is no single piece of evidence demonstrating that the HV units participated in combat against the ABiH. The Prosecution also completely disregards the fact that there were much more members of the Croatian Army who were members of the ABiH rather than of HVO, which is shown by the analysis of all documents providing data about the volunteers who left the Republic of Croatia in order to enlist with the HVO in the beginning, and then later on, when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed, they transferred into that army because there were ethnic Muslims and this was an army which defended the BiH from JNA, just like the HVO did. However, this requests a bit of analysis of all documents, and there are many documents, and numbers can be drawn from them. There is no doubt that the president, Franjo Tudjman, had a political influence on the Croatian community in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO. It's natural and logical. The Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were aware that the interests of the Republic of Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina were identical. Everyone knew that the priority was to defend themselves against the Serbian aggression, and that was also the interest of the Muslim leadership. To defend oneself against the Serbian aggression meant defending the battle-field; that is to say, the territories in both the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The aggressor was trying to occupy the areas which were covered by his plan, regardless of the existence of the borders between Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Therefore, this fact does not allow one to find some hidden motives that the Republic of Croatia had to take a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then draw from that conclusion that the Republic of Croatia assisted the HVO in its conflict with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would now also like to deal with the existence of occupation, as the Prosecution claims in its final brief. The introduction: [In English] With respect to the alleged culpability of Slobodan Praljak, due to the alleged occupation of parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina by Croatia, the Prosecution errs in their legal and factual analysis. Before examining those errors in detail, I would like to pause a moment and reflect on what the Prosecution is asking the Trial Chamber to say, from the perspective of an ordinary citizen of BiH. To the family of the volunteer who was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose multi-ethnic family is from Bosnia-Herzegovina, who took note of the Serbian aggression threatening their family and their community, who voted in local elections in which the local HDZ-BiH party won, who volunteered in one of the local multi-ethnic armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who fought and died protecting their family from the Serb aggression, to the family of that fallen veteran the Prosecution would have this Trial Chamber say, Your son was an occupier, he is merely part of a foreign -- he was merely part of a foreign occupation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If he happened to volunteer for the HVO, then he was Croatian occupier. It does not matter if he has never been to Croatia, for example. It does not matter if he or his family is ethnically Muslim or Croatian or mixed. It does not matter if his municipal force fought purely for the defence of his municipality, was organised and paid locally, and paid little regard to the orders from above the municipal level. It does not matter what he thought, or who he fought, or how he died, even if his only intent until his end was merely the defence of his own village, or perhaps a little bit broader, his municipality, from the Serb aggression, of course. The Prosecution would have Your Honours say because the evils that occur in war must be pinned on someone, and because the law and common sense are so malleable to some, your son must be found in a criminal court to be an occupier. Thousands like him must be considered foreign occupiers of their own land, the land they died for, the land they now lay beneath. Your Honours, this is not a reasonable thing for the Prosecution to ask you to say. If the same son, or his brother in a neighbouring village, had happened to volunteer for the ABiH rather than the HVO, he would not be branded as a foreign occupier by the Prosecution, despite of the foreign arms, despite of the foreign soldiers, despite the foreign influence upon the ABiH. And the Prosecution is right not to label the ABiH a foreign occupier, despite all of this. But the Prosecution is wrong to label the dead veterans of Bosnia and Herzegovina occupiers if they happen to volunteer for the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whom they do not favour at this particular trial. And we, of course, know who the Prosecutor does not favour. I think this is also errors of law. The Prosecution errs with regard to the law. It effectively assumes that because, in their mistaken opinion, they have demonstrated international armed conflict. They have also established foreign armed occupation in Croatia at the time and places where the alleged crimes occurred. This is a clear error. The existence of an international armed conflict and the existence of an occupation are separate questions. In the Naletilic trial judgement, paragraph 214, it is established that the further degree of control, then overall control, is required to establish occupation. In paragraph 218, it establishes that the Prosecution must prove beyond all reasonable doubt that the foreign power had actual control and actual authority at the relevant times and places. Influence is not merely sufficient. The Praljak Defence respectfully submits that the Government of the Republic of Croatia may have had a certain influence on both the ABiH and the HVO, given its aid to both, but the Republic of Croatia did not occupy Bosnia and Herzegovina through the HVO or, for that matter, through the ABiH. The Prosecution relies on a dissenting opinion at the International Court of Justice, Korman's separate and dissenting opinion in the Republic of Congo versus Uganda. International law, as reflected in the actual judgements of the International Court of Justice, applies stricter requirements than the dissenting opinion the Prosecution relies on. In the cited case, Congo versus Uganda, 205, paragraph 177, the ICJ held that either the state needs to have effective control over rebel groups or it needs to have direct effective control, itself, over the area. This is the proper standard. The HVO must be proved to have been effectively identical to the Croatian Army in terms of the Croatian Government's control. This cannot be proven because it was not true. The Praljak Defence respectfully refers the Trial Chamber to other important rulings on state responsibility and control of domestic armed forces, including the case Nicaragua versus the United States and Bosnia-Herzegovina versus Serbia and Montenegro. There are severe consequence if this Trial Chamber continues the fragmentation of International Law encouraged by the Prosecution. As recognised by the International Law Commission in their 2006 report on the fragmentation of International Law, on page 36, such fragmentation reduces legal security by making the law unpredictable and reduces justice because the rights of individuals depends on which jurisdiction is enforcing those rights. It is also important to emphasise the clear legal requirement that the Prosecution avoids, that in situations where fighting is still ongoing, the law of occupation does not apply. This will be addressed as I now turn to the Prosecution's errors of fact. The Prosecution erred with respect to the application of law to the facts of this case. It is characteristic of the Prosecution's approach that their final brief does not even plainly explain who the alleged occupying power is. One searches their final brief in vain for a clear phrase such as would be "the Republic of Croatia occupied Herzegovina." Perhaps it is embarrassing to actually enumerate the words. In any case, this implied, but never properly alleged, statement is clearly unproven. The Prosecution's factual analysis is based on two criteria for which, incidentally, it provides no citation in support. The first criterion is that the occupying power has rendered the occupied authorities incapable of functioning publicly or of controlling the area. This criterion happens to be the same as the first guide-line in Naletilic. Most of those guide-lines the Prosecution ignores because they do not support their allegations and they certainly cannot proven them. The second criterion is that the occupying power is in a position to exercise its authority over the territory. An objective application of the Prosecution's own criteria demonstrates that the Prosecution's assertion that Croatia occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina is in error. It certainly has not proven that Croatia occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the relevant time and did so everywhere where crimes were allegedly committed. With respect to the first criterion, that the occupying power has rendered the occupation authorities incapable of functioning publicly or of controlling the area, a few observations must be made. If we, only for the sake of discussion, imagine that the Republic of Croatia actually occupied certain territory, the question would be: Who are the occupied authorities that were rendered incapable of functioning? As said earlier, there were no functioning governmental authorities in the area. The HVO organised and gained local authority primarily because there was no effective government at all. The Prosecution, in fact, simply presumes that since the HVO established some control over certain territory within BiH borders, that it is -- that this territory was governed until then by the Sarajevo government before being taken over by the HVO. Your Honours, this presumption is wrong. There was no functioning governmental structure of BiH in those areas. The old socialist government ceased to exist or function. The new independent BiH government was not able to impose any real functional governance. The Prosecution characteristically assumes, without any actual facts or analysis, that for any particular municipality, the elected HVO government and multi-ethnic municipal defence force is the occupying power. Similarly, the party that lost the municipal elections and which actively discriminated against ethnic Croats is the, quote, "occupied power." The Praljak Defence respectfully submits that the elected HVO municipal governments, the municipal defence forces, and the institutions set up to co-ordinate between them, as best as could be managed, cannot be considered an occupying power. They were domestic, and domestic organisations do not occupy. Simple as that. It is worth bearing in mind that Slobodan Praljak was a member of both the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO. You have seen the evidence. One might ask whether the Prosecution assumes he was somehow occupying, himself, just as the local volunteers were apparently staging a foreign occupation of their own homes. The power of the HVO did not spring from foreign invasion by Croatia, as would happen in an occupation. It sprang from local grassroots efforts to manage [indiscernible]. With respect to erroneous suggestion that Croatia caused the Sarajevo government incapacity of functioning publicly or controlling the area, the Praljak Defence respectfully submits that, but for Croatia, the Sarajevo government would not have even retained the municipality -- quote, "municipality of Sarajevo," de facto power it retained during the conflict -- the only de facto power it retained during the conflict. Without Croatia's active support, the Sarajevo government would have been entirely overrun. Croatia was the anti-occupier of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the face of the very real Serb aggression. Any capacity the Sarajevo government had in the face of the Serbian onslaught was primarily because the Croatian Government provided and facilitated aid to the two co-equal BiH defence forces, the ABiH and the HVO. If one is desperate to establish the cause of the Sarajevo government's incapacity, the evidence clearly points away from Zagreb. There are obvious causes for the Sarajevo government's incapacity conspicuously absent from the Prosecution's blinkered focus on Zagreb. The Sarajevo government lacked capacity because of Belgrade, not because of Zagreb. The Sarajevo government lacked capacity because of its own failings and ethnically-biased policies. The Sarajevo government lacked capacity because the international community put it under an embargo and stood by while the Serbian aggression continued. The suggestion that the Republic of Croatia occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina at the same time that it armed and aided Bosnia-Herzegovina, should be disregarded as absurd. Similarly, even if the Prosecution proved, which it did not, that the HVO was functionally identical to the Croatian Army, which it certainly has not, does the Prosecution seriously suggest that if the local Bosnian HVO units had not formed, those areas would not have been overrun by the JNA or VRS? Had the HVO disbanded at any point, the ABiH would have been entirely overwhelmed by the JNA/VRS. The HVO was part of the BiH armed forces. This is proven, for example, by Exhibits 1D507, 2D628, 4D410, and others. The HVO saved BiH from being overrun. It did not occupy the country it saved. With respect to the second criterion identified by the Prosecution, that the so-called occupying power is in a position to exercise its authority over the territory, the Praljak Defence respectfully submits that the Prosecution simply assumes, without proof, without proof, that because the Sarajevo government was incapable, the Republic of Croatia must have had clear command and control of all areas and at all times where the alleged crimes occurred. One does not follow from the other. Just because the Sarajevo government may have been incapable at times does not mean that the Republic of Croatia was in the position to exercise its authority over the territory at the relevant places and times. Had the Prosecution intended to proven this fact, rather than assume it, the Prosecution should have proven at least two facts in each situation. First, the Prosecution should have proven that there was no fighting in the supposedly occupied territory not only between the ABiH and HVO, but also between HVO and JNA. It is not the responsibility of the Praljak Defence to demonstrate ongoing fighting, although it has. Rather, it is the obligation of the Prosecution to show that fighting has ceased in the areas it asserts were occupied. The JNA/VRS never stopped fighting. Many of the crimes alleged occurred when the ABiH attacks upon the HVO were intense. The Prosecution tends to assume conflict between the ABiH and the HVO as the norm, despite the obvious contradiction between that assumption and the assumption that there was no conflict and that the HVO was occupying in a conflict-free environment. The Prosecution failed to specifically allege or prove there was no fighting at the time crimes -- at the time crimes were allegedly committed. Accordingly, the Prosecution failed to prove occupation. Second, the Prosecution must prove that there was an unbroken chain of effective control between the Government of the Republic of Croatia to the leadership of the HVO, to the municipal governments who, themselves, were in position to exercise authority over the territory. Only then would the so-called occupying power of Croatia be able to exercise authority over the territory. Every link in that chain is broken. Influence is not command. The Republic of Croatia influenced but did not control the leadership of the HVO. The municipal forces co-operated with the top HVO leadership only when they wished to. It was not a formal, professional military with effective command, control and communication. The municipal governments, themselves, only had spotty, irregular, partial control over the essentially chaotic situation. There was no occupation here. Conclusion: Finally, the Praljak Defence must respectfully ask what this question has to do with General Slobodan Praljak. Slobodan Praljak was not king of the allegedly occupied areas. He has no criminal liability for the periods outside of his military command. During his brief period of military command, his forces were stretched to the utmost along the confrontation line, and he had no effective control outside where he was present. To place an operationally front-line commander under a regime of effective strict liability for anywhere the ABiH and JNA had not overrun would be an absurd abuse of criminal law. The Trial Chamber should resist the Prosecution efforts to push the law in this direction. Whether from the perspective of the individual Bosnian soldier, defamed as a foreign occupier, or the perspective of a volunteer member of both the HVO and the ABiH, who briefly served as a commander on the front-lines, or from the grand questions of state responsibility, the Praljak Defence respectfully submits that factual findings with respect to the subject of occupation must be approached with extreme caution. This is not only due to principles of the presumptions of innocence or in dubio pro reo. This Trial Chamber may reasonably ask itself whether the Prosecution is, in effect, putting the Republic of Croatia on trial without allowing this state to represent itself. This is a Tribunal charged with evaluating criminal culpability of natural persons, not the responsibilities of the states. It is designed to evaluate whether the Prosecution has proved a specific theory of individual criminal responsibility over specifically alleged crimes, not to ratify, broad-brush, historical generalisations which may be convenient, for technical legal reasons, for those willing to bend the law to the desired outcome. In this setting, if the Prosecution wishes to allege occupation, its allegation must be specific, and its proof must be iron-clad. Instead, the Prosecution asks this Trial Chamber to transform itself into a tribunal concerned with the responsibility of states based on rogue assertions and mostly unidentified flimsy evidence. The Prosecution asks too much of the Trial Chamber. It has failed to prove the alleged occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the international armed conflict and occupation by Republic of Croatia. It has certainly failed to prove any derivative criminal culpability of Slobodan Praljak from his false allegation of a foreign occupation. The Prosecution's allegations with respect to occupation and international armed conflict should be discarded. Your Honour, if you will allow us, my partner, Ms. Pinter, will now continue. And then, on the end, Mr. Praljak would use his 30 minutes as granted. And if you -- by your leave, we would decide on whether General Praljak will start today or on Monday. Probably, I think it would be Monday, not to pressure the things, but we'll see as the day will develop. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and around the courtroom. As Mr. Kovacic has said, in my part of the closing arguments I will analyse the Prosecution final brief. I will point out the Prosecution's erroneous interpretations and the paragraphs of their final brief that contain false allegations about the contents of documents, based on which these allegations are made, and the allegations which the Prosecution puts forward, based on quotes outside of a context, which all result in misrepresentation of the facts. I can only agree with the Prosecution in one thing, and that is their own assessment that they have not presented their case so well, because the Prosecution totally neglects the fact that the acts of which General Praljak is accused happened during a war, and the war presupposes at least two armed forces in conflict. General Praljak, who was the head of the Main Staff of the HVO, didn't wage war on the Muslim population, but with the BH Army. About what war is, and what it does to people, and how people change in war, we see what Rudy Gerritsen says in 3D991. The acts, possibilities, and the words of General Praljak must be assessed in accordance with that. The document reference is 3D991. I wish to point out the wrong interpretation of the Praljak Defence final brief. The Defence, never once, in its final brief or throughout the trial, accepted the existence of a JCE. On the contrary, the first sentence of the Defence final brief is the statement that there's no such thing as a JCE, or there was no such thing. The Defence never assumed the role of the Prosecutor and never pointed their finger at the co-accused or any other persons, shifting the blame on them. The Defence replied to the paragraphs of the indictment and pointed to documents which challenge the allegations in those paragraphs. If a paragraph of the indictment states that the authorities of the HZ-HB are responsible, according to the Prosecution, the Defence replied to that position of the Prosecution. The Defence founded its claim that General Praljak is not responsible on documents, rather than pointing their fingers at -- their finger at persons, which everybody was able to read in our final brief. General Praljak, in his testimony, never said that either Dr. Prlic or civilians were responsible for caps. And now I'll move on to the analysis of the individual paragraphs that referred to General Praljak, but I must immediately add that in this short time, I cannot deal with each and every paragraph, although each and every paragraph certainly deserves a very close review and analysis. In paragraph 42, the Prosecution implies that Praljak ordered that prisoners be withdrawn from labour on the day when he spoke to the representative of an international organisation, but immediately after that conversation, the prisoners were returned to continue labour. This is about Prozor. Siljeg, the commander of the operative zone, on 8 September 1993, ordered that prisoners be used in that way, and Praljak supposedly did nothing to make sure that this doesn't happen. The Prosecution, in this respect, cite P4256. This is a document dated 17 August 1993, although at the top of the page there's a note that it was sent by fax on 15 August 1993; in other words, two days before it was created. There is no mention in that document that the author of the document in any way spoke to General Praljak about the topic of forced labour. The Prosecution merely speculates that General Praljak's order, dated 17 August 1993, is a consequence of his meeting with the author of the document, and that, therefore, cannot be valid ground for any court decision or an assessment of General Praljak's personality. The next document is P4517, and it does not show that the author of the document spoke to General Praljak and acquainted him with the fact that prisoners have to do labour. The author of the report does not point out the status of the prisoners. The Trial Chamber has not seen evidence about the status of the detainees, whether they were prisoners of war, or detained persons, remand prisoners, military conscripts who have been isolated, civilians, or HVO members, and the status of the persons who did labour is important for the legal qualification. P9736 is another document that was supposed to corroborate the allegations of paragraph 42. This is a list of persons who worked, but the only information the Trial Chamber can draw from this document is that 20 persons worked at Jurici, and that a Muslim was in charge of these persons, and it was this Muslim who also filed a report about this event. What kind of labour this is about, we don't know. There is no evidence that on 1 September 1993, when the document was created, there were any military operations in or around Jurici. The following document that was supposed to corroborate the allegations of paragraph 42 is P4877. In no way does this document indicate that Siljeg's order was passed pursuant to General Praljak's order, nor that this document was forwarded to the Main Staff of the HVO. So how can you say that General Praljak must have known about the prisoners' or detainees' work? Document P4235, according to the Prosecution, proves that they had to use Muslims because of problems with mobilising Croats. This conclusion of the Prosecution is false. No evidence has been led that unambiguously shows that General Praljak, A, ordered, B, condoned, C, knew and failed to react to the fact that prisoners or detainees had to do work. In his testimony, General Praljak never said that any prisoner or detainee is allowed to work, nor did he say that about BH Army members who were taken prisoner. The following paragraph is 211. I would also give the reference to transcript page 51952, where the Prosecution alleges that Praljak lied with regard to the agreement with Izetbegovic and the agreement about re-subordination in connection with the decision of 15 January 1993, which has the working title, "The Ultimatum of 15 January 1993." The Prosecution failed to show evidence for the allegation that General Praljak lied. They only say that it isn't really likely that this was an oral agreement. The Prosecution says that Izetbegovic called it a potential misunderstanding which supposedly proves that General Praljak lies. The Defence would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to document P1158. It's dated 15 January 1993. These are the minutes from the office of President Tudjman. The Prosecution also cites these minutes, but what is important, with regard to General Praljak and his testimony here, can be found on page 20 of the English translation, where Gojko Susak addresses Alija Izetbegovic about talks, about re-subordination, and the reasons why he was changing his mind. I'm sure that the Trial Chamber will read these minutes and not be satisfied with the fragments that the Prosecution offers. Paragraph 233: Among other things, the Prosecution here claims that Susak threatened Izetbegovic and said that BiH would not get weapons unless Izetbegovic signs the statement. They cite document P1739 and page 26 and 27 in these minutes. There's nothing in these minutes about hostility toward the Muslims. What can be seen in these minutes is the fact that Praljak, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the knowledge and approval of Mr. Izetbegovic -- that Praljak is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The documents show that Jaganjac and Praljak are together in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that they held meetings and tried to calm down the situation to prevent a conflict between allies. They are reducing tensions. Praljak had done that since late October 1992, while he was in and around Prozor, Vakuf and Travnik. We also mention this in our final brief. With regard to the threat, according to the Prosecution, I must say that the threat was not about signing the agreement on re-subordination, but about Konjic, which can be seen from P1739 again. At that time, attacks on the HVO started in Konjic, and on 20 March 1993 the representatives of the BH Army strike an agreement that they don't want to be together with the HVO again. The document reference is 2D00253. In paragraph 242, which refers to the second ultimatum of 15 April 1993, the Prosecution cite document P1942, dated 19 April 1993. This exhibit was led through Witness Okun, and I would like to point out the conclusion of that document, which says: "The situation is critical, and while the highest -- or before the highest civilian authorities in BiH take action to resolve the situation, there can be no hope of a peaceful solution in the near future." Document P2458, which is the Mazowiecki report of 19 May 1993, under item 7, says: "The strategic importance of the Lasva Valley, in accordance to the planned Province 10, Croatian majority administrative centre in Travnik, the Muslims are not willing to accept that." So the documents of the Prosecution side show that the peace between the Muslims and the Croats depended on the Muslims. "The displacement of Bosnian Croats orchestrated by Tudjman," that's the heading from the final brief of the Prosecution. In paragraph 262 through 293, they deal with this. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas dealt with this topic and analysed the witnesses. I want to analyse the documents on which the Prosecution base their allegations. Paragraph 276 through 292 speak about the HVO propaganda that Muslim crimes have been committed, whereas reports from the ground state that there has been a little bit of firing, with few casualties. Reports speak that thousands of Croats from Travnik were being transferred at night and clandestinely. There's a footnote reference to Azra Krajsek. The transcript page is 20114, and it says that nobody confirmed having seen any Mujahedin. But the UN reports, the reports of observers and other documents, clearly show that Mujahedins did very much take part in the operation. Witness Filipovic, upon the questions of Judge Antonetti, confirmed their presence, and the transcript page is 47561 and the following, as well as 47 -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevant documents are 2D1407; 2D1262; P6697, page 7, paragraphs 29 and 30; 3D1914; 4D597; 3D331. And I repeat the number that wasn't recorded, 2D1407. The consequences of defensive activities of the BH Army were the following: The fall of Bugojno and a river of Croats who had fled Bugojno and, before that, the Croats who had fled Kakanj and Travnik. They didn't come to Prozor, or Rama, or Vares, and later to Herzegovina, because that was a result of propaganda, but they were saving their bare lives, which was also described by Witness Filipovic. The Prosecution mention Filipovic's answer in paragraph 292. However, the answer that the Prosecution cite to confirm their thesis is Filipovic's answer to the question about document 4D567, which was recorded on page 47556. That's a map which was showed to him depicting the situation in November 1993 and the refugees. General Filipovic's answer was: "Don't abandon your homes unless your lives are in danger." General Filipovic's answer to the question -- to that question cannot be a plausible argument for the Prosecution and can by no means be linked to the retreat of the Croats due to propaganda and orchestrated reverse ethnic cleansing. Starting from June 1993, during the BH Army offensive, the population of Croats in Travnik was reduced by 20.000; in Kakanj, by 15.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "20.000"]; in Bugojno, by 15.000. The Croats didn't leave Central Bosnia to implement the policy of the JCE, but due to the fierce offensive of the BH Army against areas inhabited by Croats. The fear of the BH Army and its operations, rather than the HVO propaganda, caused the escape of the Croats. And I would like to correct what has been recorded. The figure for Kakanj was 15.000. The Croats did not leave Travnik, Kakanj, Bugojno and Vares of their own free will. They were saving their lives, escaping before the attacks of the BH Army, not to implement Franjo Tudjman's and Slobodan Praljak's objective, which would also be their own objective, because if they were leaving of their own free will, then they would also be protagonists of the JCE. The evidence shows something else, though: Exhibit 1D1654, the third amended indictment in the Hadzihasanovic case, P3337, 3D837, 3D1731, 2D1407, 3D2632, 3D2775. With regard to that part of the final brief of the Prosecution about Ljubuski, Stolac and Capljina, I would like to point to paragraph 353 and an allegation in it about the establishment of Croatian rule, language, school curriculums, and flying the Croatian flag. This is a description of the conduct of the HVO toward the Muslims, and it's about Croat-isation. Let me first say that the flag in question was not the flag of the Republic of Croatia. It was the flag of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to draw the Chamber's attention to document 3D3228, "Hercegovacki Vojnik," or "Herzegovinian Soldier." That was a publication of the 4th Corps BH Army from February 1993. The document number is 3228. The document describes the events of 1993, the shelling of Mostar and Stolac; 23 January 1993, Stolac shelled by VRS; 24 January 1993, Stolac shelled by VRS; 1 February, attacks on Stolac, over 500 shells fired on the lines and 20 on the town of Stolac; 2 February 1993, a continuation of the attack on Stolac. They were able to defend Stolac together with the HVO. That's what the publication says. They also mention Pocitelj and 12.000 civilians who were transferred. We listened -- we heard about that during the trial. Fierce fighting ensued, and on Bajram the lily flag flew from the mosque. Luburic, a Croat, brought the first lilies. That's what the 4th Corps says. I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to review this document, too, when it analyses the testimonies of the witnesses in this Trial Chamber about the HVO attacking Stolac, shelling it, destroying it, and Croat-ising it. Your Honours, I will now move on to the criminal responsibilities of Slobodan Praljak from Chapter 11 of the Prosecution final brief, so this may be a convenient moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I stopped at the criminal responsibility of General Praljak, which is described in Chapter 11 of the Prosecution final brief, and the paragraphs are 614 through 860. I will only discuss the elements which I believe are important. In paragraph 649, the Prosecution claims that the Convicts Battalion was also known under the title ATG Tuta and that General Praljak commanded the Convicts Battalion. The claim is supported with P4134 and 4131. However, considering the ATG Tuta and the Convicts Battalion as one and the same is something that the Prosecution also states in paragraph 296 of the final brief. The documents do not confirm that it's possible to consider the Convicts Battalion and the ATG Tuta as one and the same. Not a single piece of evidence originating from the time when General Praljak was the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO indicate that, by his orders, he issued any task to the Convicts Battalion. The Prosecution has not presented evidence that would demonstrate that the Convicts Battalion was in Rastani on the orders of the Main Staff of the HVO, nor did it present a single piece of evidence which would rebut the Defence claim that Mladen Naletilic was not the commander of the ATG Tuta. On the contrary, Exhibit 4D01356 is an interview with Ivan Andabak, who confirmed that the Convicts Battalion, when it was engaged in war in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, was only subordinated to Mate Boban, and evidence to the contrary has not been presented to the Court. In the document P05226, and the date is the 20th of September, 1993, a letter of the chief of Security Sector of the Defence Department, addressed to Mate Boban and concerning a serious incident caused by the members of the Convicts Battalion, it is noted that the convicts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Convicts Battalion was under the command of the Main Staff of the HVO, then this letter would have been addressed to the Main Staff of the HVO, rather than to Mate Boban. If the chief of the Security Sector had been under the command of the Main Staff of the HVO, i.e., Slobodan Praljak, then he would have addressed the letter to Slobodan Praljak, as his commander, rather than write to Mate Boban, side-stepping his own commander. The Main Staff never received this document. The Prosecutor has not presented a single piece of evidence on the basis of which the Trial Chamber could establish with certainty that Slobodan Praljak was informed with the events in Ljubuski which are referred to in the document. The document undoubtedly demonstrates that the Convicts Battalion was under the command of Mate Boban, as General Praljak, indeed, claimed in his testimony. Document P7009 is a payroll for the month of November 1993, for the members of the Convicts Battalion and the ATG. These were the anti-terrorist units. It shows that ATG Tuta is not mentioned as a unit that was a part of the Convicts Battalion or that the Convicts Battalion was one and the same as the ATG Tuta. The conclusion that the ATG Tuta was one and the same as the Convicts Battalion cannot be drawn from the contents of the document that the Prosecution refers to. The Prosecution did not provide a single piece of evidence that would indicate that the Convicts Battalion and the ATG Tuta can be considered one and the same. No evidence was presented indicating that this was the same military unit, and a criminal procedure cannot include any assumptions or speculation. Contrary to the allegations made in paragraph 654 and in transcript page 51880 - the date is Tuesday, the 8th of February, 2011 - in which the Prosecution expressly relies on the testimony of Generals Petkovic and Filipovic and claims that there was no problems with command, control and communications within the HVO, the one page, 51935, it adds that there were also no problems within the chain of command, the Defence points to the claims from its final brief, Chapter 16, in which the Defence of General Praljak shows, in the documents and witness testimonies, that command, control, and the system of communications within the HVO were insufficient and not fully established. The testimony of General Petkovic, which the Prosecution disregards, and which is recorded on page 40363 of the transcript, confirms the arguments of General Praljak's Defence. This is recorded, I mean, General Praljak's testimony, on page 44121 and 41138. A very precise picture about the existence of 3C elements within the HVO was provided to the Trial Chamber by Witness Skender, and this is something that he experienced personally, and the same thing follows from his statement, 3D3710. As for the quality of the communications, document P4698A, page 86, talks about this. In paragraph 661, it is noted that Dr. Tudjman appointed Praljak to be one of those who would relay the policy of Herceg-Bosna, that is to say, the Croatian Government about the Banovina, to Izetbegovic until the exclusion of the government in Sarajevo. The Prosecution incorrectly mentions this claim, because in paragraph -- in document P00 -- P00524, on page 23, there is no such text. It has been added. When the transcript is read in its entirety, it can be established that it has to do with talks about the annex to the agreement about co-operation with the BiH, and on page 23, appointment of persons on the Croatian side is mentioned to the joint committee charged with the implementation of this agreement. Praljak and Bobetko have been proposed. However, on page 23 that the Prosecution refers to, President Tudjman said: "As for Izetbegovic, we'll tell him openly, when he comes here, what we said at the very beginning." Sarajevo is never mentioned, nor is it ever mentioned that General Praljak will relay to Alija Izetbegovic what was said, as the Prosecution claims. President Tudjman is, rather, the person who will talk with Mr. Izetbegovic, whereas General Praljak has not been appointed to relay any message. For the sake of argument, I want to note that if General Praljak was a member of the committee charged with the implementation of the annex to the agreement, then it's only logical that he should advocate the positions of the side which he is representing, and there is no criminal activity in this. This document shows that there was no hypocritical policy from the Croatian side in relation to Alija Izetbegovic, because Dr. Tudjman decided to inform Mr. Izetbegovic about the position of the Republic of Croatia. In the next sentence of paragraph 661, it is noted that at the meeting held on the 5th of November, 1993, Praljak confirmed that the goal was to secure the area within the borders of the Banovina that would be controlled by the Croats, and the Prosecution conclusion, on the basis of this document, is that it is out of the question that achieving this goal did not request movement of the population and, in particular, reducing the number of the Muslim population in a large part of Herceg-Bosna. Document P6454 that the Prosecution refers to, page 50 - it's one of the presidential transcripts - shows that this sentence which is quoted in the above paragraph has been taken out of the context of the whole speech and also out of the context of the events which preceded. The speech should be read in its entirety, and it's recorded on pages 47 through to 57 of the English translation. When you read the entire text, you can conclude that General Praljak is describing the military situation, and discusses military positions, and analyses events in Vakuf and Central Bosnia in connection with the offensive launched by the Army of BiH, its military power and political ideas to create a Muslim state. It can be concluded from the text of this speech that the Prosecution claim from the above paragraph is an assumption which cannot be included in the criminal procedure because nothing confirms it. As for the context in which these talks were held, I wish to indicate the document P04027. That's the agreement on humanitarian convoys from Makarska. The HVO authorities were facing the refugees and displaced persons from Central Bosnia. 42.000 of them and another 8.000 were expected to arrive from Kakanj and Vares. As the Defence already emphasised a number of times, the events cannot be considered in isolation, but in their entirety, and we should not forget for a moment that everything is taking place in the context of at least two wars which are being waged simultaneously. In paragraph 262, there is a claim that Praljak advocated a policy in relation to BiH which implied a joint criminal enterprise, and what is noted here is a secret meeting in Hungary held on the 5th of October, 1992, with Ratko Mladic, and another meeting with Ratko Mladic three weeks after that, as well as a meeting which General Praljak had with a French delegation in January 1993, and, finally, a meeting held on the 2nd of April, 1993, where Praljak briefed the military commanders in an authoritarian manner, according to what is stated in this paragraph. The documents that the Prosecution refers to -- that is to say, some parts of these documents that it refers to, cannot prove these claims, because they are taken out of context and they lead to a wrong conclusion. The Prosecutor also refers to the document P11376 and P11380, Mladic's diary. As for these exhibits, the Trial Chamber was not told whether General Praljak was present or whether he participated in these discussions, and if he did, with what status, because, supposedly, what was discussed during the meeting was the Republic of Croatia ending the attack on Slavonski Brod and ending war operations in the Republic of Croatia. General Praljak did not have the opportunity to face the author of this note and hear his testimony or cross-examine him, nor did he have an opportunity to testify about the contents of these notes from the meeting which was supposedly held. Therefore, the Defence notes that these documents have no probative value because they were not tested by examination. This is hearsay evidence, mainly the monologues of one side in the talks, whereas there is no information about what the other side in these talks stated. The Defence wrote in detail about these exhibits in its final brief, so I will not talk about them anymore. In paragraph 662, document P9447 is also mentioned. It is page 8, and it is an interview which General Praljak gave after the war. The Prosecution claims that the general said that the policy of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina was closer to Croats than the Muslim policy; unity is out of the question. During the trial, the Prosecution also played the video-recording of this interview. In this way, the Prosecution wanted to connect General Praljak with the Army of Republika Srpska and a criminal agreement with Mladic. But as the Prosecutor wrote, it was not to the detriment of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but to the detriment of the Muslims. It was said several times already that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not the property of Muslims; it is a state which belongs equally to the Muslims, Croats and Serbs. The allegation made in the footnote does not exist in the original document and has not been recorded in the trial transcript of the 8th of February, 2011, during the oral presentation of my learned friend Mr. Scott, during which he also played the video with interview given by General Praljak. The text of the transcript of the video in Croatian is recorded on page 11 of document P9447, and the sentence, "Unity is out of the question," is never mentioned in it. Correction of the translation: Had been requested so it would be harmonised with the original text. The sentences that the Prosecution refers to are taken out of context, and the full answer, as it is recorded in the text, mentions the military alliance with Muslims before the war, but differences with regard to political options and configuring the joint state. The Prosecution claim that Praljak co-operated with Mladic is arbitrary, unfounded and incorrect. Footnote 1538 includes the reference that in January 1993, General Praljak informed the French delegation that the Banovina is an area which belongs to the Croats. Incorrect. 3D482, which is the document that the Prosecution refers to, says the following: that General Praljak said this: "The territory which belongs to the Croats corresponds with the borders of the Banovina Hrvatska from the configuration of Yugoslavia in 1939 and is in harmony with the census from 1981, because the 1991 census has not been recognised. Croats advocate a single and unified BiH as a state and for the rights of Croats as a constitutive people. The problems between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina are a result of different goals of political struggle. The Croats are struggling for the state of BiH, with autonomy for the Croats, whereas the Muslims are struggling for a civil state." The Defence wishes to refer to the document P10463. It is an interview given by Mr. Izetbegovic in which he says: "We only have the possibility to achieve the ideal of a civil republic or a civil war." Document 1D2479 explains what a civil state means, according to the proposal of the SDA and Mr. Izetbegovic. One vote per one man. This position completely disregards the constitutive peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, finally, the last document which is supposed to confirm an allegation, paragraph 662, that Praljak exerted authority on briefing HVO commanders is document P1788, pages 1 through 3. The Prosecutor quotes from the document, but we encounter a problem here. The quote, as a compilation of two different generals, provided by General Praljak to two different questions - one of them was about Vares and the other one about Posavina - the mere fact that General Praljak confirmed that he, indeed, had attended that meeting does not confirm the credibility of the minutes and the contents thereof. I would permittedly like to point out the probative value of this document, which we highlighted during trial every time when the document came up. We don't know who drafted the minutes. We don't know how capable the note-taker was to understand the topic. And General Praljak, who spoke about the Vance-Owen Peace Plan and presented his positions and analysis of what might happen in the future as a result of that plan, we don't know whether he managed to catch all of the general's words. We don't know whether the minutes are just a summary of all the interventions. We don't know anything about how the document came to be. The text is illegible, and when shown to General Praljak, General Praljak, himself, said that he could not read the document, and that the text which was shown to him does not reflect any of his words. During trial, the general stated his position and challenged the accuracy of the minutes; i.e., he said that his words were not properly noted. The Defence would like to point out that General Praljak described and interpreted what was said at the meeting. He repeated that before the Trial Chamber in response to the honourable Judge Antonetti's questions, as well as in response to the Prosecutor's question. Everything that was said about the credibility of the document and the contents thereof is recorded on the transcript pages 43381 through 43410, that is, Mr. Slobodan Praljak's testimony, as well as 43675, again General Praljak's testimony. This was also recorded on transcript pages when Witness EA testified on pages 24363 through 24376, as well as on the transcripts of Witness William Tomljanovich's words, the pages are 6062 through 6072 on the 19th of September, 2006. A suggested, implied, an erroneous interpretation of any document must not be allowed to lead to erroneous conclusions on the part of the Trial Chamber in criminal proceedings. In paragraph 663, to corroborate the claim that Praljak complained about the fact that achieving a Croatian state in the HR-HB fades and weakens, the Prosecution refers to document P6454. This is the Split minutes, a meeting with President Tudjman, but again we have an erroneous interpretation on the part of the Prosecutor. General Praljak did not speak about the achievement of a Croatian state in the HR-HB, which is the liberal interpretation on the part of the Prosecution, but here, intrinsically and exclusively to the text, we can establish that the general made a comparison between the leaderships of the Serbs, Muslims and Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when he came to describe the Croats, he concluded, and I quote it: "In that respect, Mr. President, we started resembling, all of us together, a collective of farmers." The text has to be presented as a whole, not as fragments. I expect that the Trial Chamber will not reduce evidence to its mere fragments. In paragraph 664, the Prosecution claims that Praljak, himself, recognised that he had the de facto command power even before he was appointed commander. The Prosecution refers to General Praljak's testimony recorded on the transcript pages quoted in the footnote. However, the quoted pages do not confirm the allegations in that paragraph. On those pages, Praljak did not admit that he was the de facto commander. Actually, he expressly said that he did not have any command authorities, and while he was not a commander, he had authority while assisting HVO units. The Prosecutor refers to document P8838 when describing General Praljak's command authorities, and he is referring to page 4. This is a document which was created on the 2nd of April, 1998, in Sarajevo on OBN Television. In a TV studio, General Praljak gave an interview. However, when we look at the interview, we will not see that a reference was made to General Praljak's authorities. We can only hear that Praljak said that his lads respected him and loved him, but that has nothing to do with his command authorities. In paragraph 664, Praljak's high position in the HVO and close relationship with Tudjman provided him with de facto power. That's not correct. Praljak did not have authority in HVO among soldiers because of his close relations with President Tudjman. He had built his authority and respect himself. I would be curious to know how closeness may be considered as an element of a crime, and what legal category would that constitute? In paragraph 665, numerous documents show that Praljak was, from October 1992 to July 1993, the de facto commander of the HVO units' commanders and civilian leaders as their superior. Documents to which the Prosecutor refers do not confirm this allegation, because the generals co-signed those documents together with somebody who, indeed, had the authority. When we talk about the role of General Praljak in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is something that we have been listening to for five years in this courtroom, from Praljak and the Prosecutor's witnesses. I would like to point to a document, 3D3510, which is General Praljak's military booklet that he received from Arif Pasalic, and based on which he was a member of the BiH Army. The Prosecutor refers to document P9838, talking about the de facto command authority of Mr. Praljak. This document is under seal. I'm not going to say what's in the document. I'm just going to mention the initials of the witness. Document 9838 is the transcript of Witness Z's testimony in the Martinovic/Naletilic case. The same witness appeared in our case under pseudonym CU. The Prosecution refers to P9838, and we have to say that General Praljak did not participate in that case as an accused, he did not have a possibility to cross-examine the witness and challenge his testimony. This witness did testify in our case, he was cross-examined, and if the Prosecutor believes that the witness provided a testimony which was relevant for this case, then he should have referred to the relevant pages of the transcript. In paragraph 666, the Prosecution speaks about Coric, who had accepted as a fait accompli Praljak's appointment of a higher HVO officer of the military police. And the reference for that is document P00927. This document speaks about the de jure and not the de facto authority, because it speaks about the appointment -- or the appointment of a person which, in the month of April 1992, arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina and was appointed as a commander of the military police in the OG South-East Herzegovina. At that time, General Praljak was the chief of staff of the OG. At that time, General Praljak was the chief of the South-East Herzegovina OG, so this document cannot confirm the allegations in the paragraph about the de facto authorities. It was just -- it was the de jure authority. Praljak never denied that he arrived even before his formal appointment. What General Praljak said was that he was not a commander with all the authorities pertaining to a commander, but rather he assisted, and he had an ability to influence troops because of a relationship that he had built before. In paragraph 668, Praljak is portrayed as being centrally involved in planning, and with his authority, as a senior commander, he contributed to the important meetings of his subordinates. To corroborate that, the Prosecution proposes document P01350, the meeting that was held on the 29th of January, 1993, with the military police. Praljak did not chair that meeting. He merely responded to the questions about Vakuf, Central Bosnia. He was at the meeting -- or he was in Vakuf and Central Bosnia because of the problems there. And he also spoke about the situation in Croatia, about Zadar, Maslenica. Praljak was not in a position to receive reports from the military police, as the paragraph suggests, so the military police never reported to Praljak. Paragraph 669 says that the official communications of the HVO recognised Praljak's pivotal role in the chain of command even before the 24th of July, 1993. This should be corroborated by document P1311. I will kindly ask the Trial Chamber to read the document in its entirety, especially when they decide about the part of the indictment that concerns Gornji Vakuf, because the document reads: "The BiH Army forces in Vakuf in the January conflict made up 4.300 members of the BiH Army which participated in the conflict." And then there is a list of all the units which had arrived in Gornji Vakuf. This is 5(L) in the document. On page 3 of the document, it says: "During the writing of the report, I was informed about the instructions that Zrinko Tokic received from Brada, and I shall act accordingly." Based on this sentence alone, the Trial Chamber cannot conclude that General Praljak had a pivotal role in command. The role of General Praljak was explained in our final brief and concerns the area of Gornji Vakuf and Uskoplje. The following document that the Prosecution proposes to prove the pivotal role of General Praljak in the command chain is P02039. This is Mico Lasic's report about the condition in Konjic and Jablanica on the 22nd of April, 1993. It was submitted to the Main Staff and to General Praljak as well. Praljak testified that he had been in Mostar to attend reconciliation talks in April 1993. He attended talks at the SDA, and he also spoke to Pasalic. The Trial Chamber was shown Mustafa Hadrovic's photos. He took photos of General Praljak together with Arif Pasalic, and that's on pages 14613 through 14616 of the transcript. General Praljak came to Mostar to appease tensions between Muslims and Croats. This is illustrated by 3D3261, which is Slobodan Bozic's statement. He spoke about General Praljak's arrival in Mostar in order to appease tensions. The following document that corroborates the allegations in the paragraph according to the Prosecution is P02092. Brada asked for Tuta to come back to him. What conclusions can be made about Praljak's pivotal role in the chain of command as we read this document? If he had, indeed, had a central role in the command, then he would not use a mediator to ask Tuta to come back to him. There is no data whatsoever as to what that document refers to, and that document cannot be used to establish either a positive or a negative fact. The international community was -- filed a formal complaint with regard to Praljak's authorities on 23rd April 1993. This is what the Prosecution claims, and this is supported by document P02043. Arif Pasalic filed a complaint on the 23rd of April, 1993, immediately before he had taken a stroll along the east bank of Mostar and had a cup of coffee in a bar in East Mostar. He filed that complaint, where he says that due to the stay of General Praljak, the complaint is being filed, but that didn't bother him then, that didn't bother him in 1993. Documents IC443 and IC444 are documents which were received from Witness Hadrovic, and they depict General Praljak in the company of Arif Pasalic and other members both of the HVO and the BiH Army in Mostar in the month of April 1993. On the 14th of November, 1992, Arif Pasalic writes: "Units of the ABiH and the HVO Herceg Stjepan unit elaborated a plan of action in very great detail against the Army of Republika Srpska." They are waiting for an order to arrive from Mr. Praljak. We can conclude from this document that Praljak was in command of both the HVO and the ABiH units. And this document also challenges the allegation that Praljak considerably contributed and participated in the joint criminal enterprise in Herceg-Bosna. Paragraph 673 is in the chapter entitled "Praljak's Transformation from De Facto Commander to De Jure Commander." That paragraph says: "It has been decided to change Praljak's status in an attempt to cover up his role of a Croatian agent in the support of the Herceg-Bosna JCE." Before analysing the document, let me just point out that at no time the stay of General Praljak in Bosnia-Herzegovina was hidden or kept secret, and that international representatives and, of course, Alija Izetbegovic knew of his presence. By the way, upon Izetbegovic's request, Praljak came to BiH, and he had met with him before he became commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. General Praljak never denied his involvement with the HZ-HB, but we must look at the time when this conversation happened comparatively. In mid-June, the BH Army, which now openly advances against the HVO and attacks Kakanj and Travnik, the possibility of joint action is no more there. The international community exerts pressure on the Republic of Croatia because of the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but not on those who are advancing, whose offensive it is. The Muslims, except for a military offensive, have also launched a propaganda and political offensive. They turned against their allies because they are now ready for the Croats. This is shown in document P1325 of 27 January 1993, page 5. It is for this very propaganda and political offensive that there is whining about the presence of the HV and BiH. In that situation, although General Praljak, until that time, had for eight months tried to prevent the war with the BH Army, he became a person being pointed at -- just like now in the indictment, the person pointed at, as the representative of Croatian BiH, to rule out objections, General Praljak couldn't be forbidden to defend his country, and to prevent him from being used as a proof of the involvement of Croatia in the conflict with the BH Army, his release from the Croatian Army would resolve his status in BiH. But it is important to point out that there can be no talk of a retroactive appointment, because General Praljak became commander on 24 July 1993, and the aforementioned meeting took part in June, which means a month earlier. Once again, let me point out that nobody ever tried to cover up General Praljak's presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Central Bosnia, or in Herzegovina before his formal appointment, nor did anyone -- Praljak. There was no reason for that. In paragraph 675, it is alleged that there were regular contacts with Tudjman and Susak so that he may inform them of the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army, and for him to get instructions for him about the JCE and its implementation. But the Prosecution doesn't offer any documents or any citations to substantiate this allegation, for the simple reason that there are no documents of this kind. Then it says he was the channel for information, demands, policies and feedback between the Croatian leadership and the HVO/HZ-HB with regard to the JCE.
