The document mentioned in this context is P1622, dated 9 March 1993. The pages are 18, 42, 36 of the presidential transcript. Susak speaks to the representatives of Central Bosnia, who want Praljak to return to introduce order again, and Susak says that Praljak will return. In March, Praljak was in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the knowledge of Izetbegovic, who never once demanded that Praljak be withdrawn from HZ-HB. If he was sent to BiH to appease the situation, then it's normal that he should inform those who sent him there. General Praljak was in contact with Izetbegovic, which follows from General Praljak's testimony but also from the minutes of 27 March 1993, which is P1739. Praljak exercised de jure command and control after 24 July 1993. In paragraph 681, the Prosecution say: "Praljak said that he was responsible if he failed to react to wrong acts by Petkovic and Tole, as well as anybody else's." And there is a reference to a transcript page. However, on these pages, General Praljak actually said: "Under the conditions that we had, and considering the communication that we had and the type of war that went on, if anybody proves that I violated any provision of International Law, I am willing to bear full responsibility for it, as I said at the very beginning." That's what General Praljak said, and it's up to the Prosecution to prove that the general did not react to wrongdoings or failures, although he knew that they were committed. In paragraph 683, it says, Praljak's subordinates recognised his command authority, which extended to the HVO MP and the civilian police. What would an army be like if it were not to recognise or acknowledge the command authority of the commander of the Main Staff, which is proved by that claim? It would be -- it would have been fortunate if Praljak's subordinate had obeyed and fully respected the orders issued by General Praljak. More detail about this is in our final brief, "Command Responsibility 3C." The following document is P5405 of 26 September 1993, information for Mr. Praljak about the civilian convoy from Vares being halted, but this document doesn't belong with this footnote, nor does it have anything to do with General Praljak, because this is about civilian affairs. Document P6095, also cited by the Prosecution, does not confirm the allegations in the paragraph, because it isn't about either the civilian or the military police. Document P6360 of 2 November 1993, an attack order, has nothing to do with the military police or the civilian police. They are not involved in combat activities, nor are they mentioned in the order. This document refers to an area not covered by the indictment, at a time after General Praljak had become commander, so even in this respect it is irrelevant. The command authority of the commander of the Main Staff, in itself, cannot be considered an element of the commission of a criminal offence unless it is linked with an illegal act. General Praljak or his Defence never denied that General Praljak had command authority, but they did deny the allegation that this command authority was used to commit crimes. But whatever the Prosecution have to add -- to show during the trial or with these documents does not refute this claim of the Defence. The Prosecution seek to confirm the allegation that Praljak's command authority was extended to include the military police. It is based on some documents. But the Praljak Defence never denied that when the military police was under the Main Staff or the operative zone, that they were under their command. In this part of the Prosecution brief about Praljak's authority over the military police, they mention document P3829. I am now shortening because I have no time to go into the details of each and all documents. They say that Praljak reacts to unlawful acts when he learns of them, and he asks to be informed of them. Praljak has contacts with representatives of international organisations, which is also mentioned by the Prosecution. He also has contacts with the UNPROFOR and certainly must have information about measures taken to be able to forward that information. By his request and warning, Praljak only showed that at all times he demanded disciplinary proceedings to be launched and discipline to be implemented from those who can -- who are in a position to do so. In paragraph 688, the Prosecution claim that when Boban issued the order of 15 September 1993 to the armed forces to comply with International Law, Praljak implemented Boban's order and sent it to the chief of the Military Police Administration. Two paragraphs refer to the entire military police. That is a misinterpretation of document P5104. This document was first -- was addressed first to the Department of Defence and then, secondly, to the Main Staff. With regard to this document, I would like to say that the correct translation of this document can be found on transcript page 44309. During General Praljak's testimony, the correct translation of the document was verified. And Slobodan Praljak included Boban's order in his order, and it can be found in document P5188. General Praljak again orders that International Law be complied with. Document P5104 shows that possibly some detention centres do not provide adequate conditions, but this document does not inform Slobodan Praljak of any breaches of International Humanitarian Law. On 9 February 2011, the Prosecution puts forward its allegations with regard to their evidence. They say that General Praljak knew everything at all times. This was recorded on transcript page 51925. To prove their allegations, the Prosecution identifies three documents, but if we read these documents, we see that General Praljak was not the one who had information about the events about which these documents speak. These documents do not refer to Slobodan Praljak, nor do they indicate any concrete knowledge of specific mis-treatment. The Prosecution never precisely showed -- identified a document that shows that Praljak must have known any specific fact at any point in time. In their final brief, the Prosecution sought to show that General Praljak knew some facts by showing maps, which is very unusual in criminal proceedings, I must say. What does the Prosecution say? Praljak was probably in command in Prozor a few days before and a few days after the representative of an international organisation was there. He must have been there when the representative of that international organisation was there, and he must have known what the representative of that organisation knew. They cite document 3D981 and 3D979 in that context. These documents only show that representatives of international organisations were allowed access to prisons. The Prosecution claim that the military police were deployed in Prozor to implement the objectives of the JCE, but that claim is unfounded. The Prosecution says the battalions were deployed in various areas where HVO forces committed various crimes from the indictment. It is uncontested that military police battalions were re-subordinated to the commander of the operations zone in combat operations. We discussed that in the final brief. Mr. Coric could deploy them and order their re-subordination. However, these documents do not deal with the crime which was committed in the territory where these units were engaged, nor does the Prosecution indicate which crime this would be. In Prozor and Vakuf, the HVO defended itself from the attack of the Army of BiH, so it is difficult to connect their defensive position with the advancement of a joint criminal enterprise. In paragraph 690, the Prosecution claims that Praljak issued orders to the military police units on the 4th of August, 1993, and the 20th of September, 1993, throughout the relevant period, or immediately before the commission of the crimes listed in the indictment. Context should be given for the documents listed in the footnote to this paragraph. Document 3D2613, dated the 20th of September, 1993, talks about the duration of the offensive called "Neretva 93" in the area of Prozor/Rama. Axes of ABiH operations are described. The document was created just a few days after the massacre in Uzdol, in which 29 civilians were killed by the BiH Army. Another document that talks about the duration of the offensive in the Rama area is 1D00541, "Sefer Halilovic's Cunning Strategy: The Truth About Uzdol." In it, a direct participant in the offensive describes the axis of attack, the actions that were carried out, the units which were involved, and claims that Neretva 93 was not a private operation, but an operation planned by the General Staff and personally approved by General Rasim Delic. One of the axes in this operation was Here-Uzdol, and it was led by the Independent Prozor Battalion, commanded by Buzo, who was awarded for this operation by being promoted. In view of the consequences of this offensive of the Army of BiH, in view of the casualties which were a consequence of this action in Uzdol, General Praljak, in order to prevent the further killing of civilians, and to successfully repel a fierce offensive, requested that military police should also be engaged, but the question here is: What crimes did the HVO commit in defending itself against the attack, as the Prosecution provides no answers? The Defence points to document P5162, dated the 17th of September, 1993, which says that in spite of the massacre in Uzdol, the Croats in Prozor did not abuse Muslims. Document P4260, quoted in footnote 1604 -- it says the following: "Praljak ordered the military police, on the 17th of August, 1993, to withdraw prisoners from the works in Prozor and bring them back, by which he showed that he commanded the military police, in terms of prisoner issues." Praljak's order, dated the 17th of August, 1993, according to the Prosecutor, indicates that Slobodan Praljak was aware of the possibility that the prisoners were working in Rama from that date onwards. The order shows his will to try and eliminate the possibility of having the prisoners work, even though this was not his responsibility, particularly with regard to document P04285, which is the reply of Ante Pavlovic dated the 18th of August, 1993. It is a response to the order of General Praljak. It could not show him in any way that forced labour was still going on. The Prosecutor has not managed to prove that Slobodan Praljak was aware that prisoners did any work. Indeed, he had no reason to think so, but rather had reason to think, as he was informed, that they did not. The Prosecutor does not accept the possibility that this practice could have been concealed from Slobodan Praljak, as he had prohibited such practice. In paragraph 710, the Prosecution refers to an interview by General Praljak and says that Praljak admitted that he consulted the political leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. According to the Prosecution, this is confirmed by document P8765. The author is Nebojsa Taraba, who interviewed Slobodan Praljak, and the title of this article is "I'm Not Responsible." The Prosecution refers to page 4. However, in page 4, on the first sentence of the paragraph, there is nothing to indicate any unlawful activity. The Defence, however, points out that this is an interview for which we do not know whether it was authorised, and whether the words of General Praljak were correctly recorded, and whether his words unseen are correct. There is nothing unlawful in consultation with leaders of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. What the Prosecution lacks, if any weight is to be given to this claim, is evidence that in these statements any crime was ever agreed or planned. The claim from the second sentence of this paragraph, namely, that Praljak took part in the meetings in top leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, showing that his acts and decisions fit the broader picture of the general HVO and HZ-HB policy, is a Prosecution claim not supported by evidence. There is even no reference given to support the claim. In footnote 1648, the following claim is included: The soldiers which joined the HVO remained on the payroll of the Croatian Army. And reference is given to the page of transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the transcript page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say the following here, and point to the general's testimony which is recorded on page 43039, that the volunteers from the Croatian Army were treated in the same way if they enlisted with the BiH Army, the Muslims, which is confirmed by document 3D00299. Another document is used by the Prosecution in order to show the presence of the Croatian Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, more particularly, in Herceg-Bosna. I have to refer to it because it is a completely wrong interpretation. The Prosecution refers to the document P03917, and the footnote is 1648, where the Prosecution says that this document confirms the presence of the Croatian Army, but this is, rather, the unit Hrvoje Vukcic Hrvatinic and the return of the unit Hrvoje Vukcic Hrvatinic from Jajce. "HV," as written before "Hrvatinic," does not stand for "Croatian Army." During all these years that we have been sitting in this courtroom, and we have seen so many documents on the basis of which the Prosecution may have realised that once you say "Croatian Army," and put the abbreviation "HV," there are never any full stops in this abbreviation. In this document, however, the "HV," "Hrvatinic," there is a full stop after the "H", because the "H" stands for the name "Hrvoje." Therefore, proving something by this document, the Prosecution could in no way have proved the presence of the Croatian Army in Herceg-Bosna. In paragraph 718, the Prosecution claims that on 16th of January, 1993, the commander of the North-Western Operations Zone reported that Praljak had sent a message to the Army of BiH that they would be destroyed unless they accept the decision of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The HVO negotiators in Gornji Vakuf also consulted Praljak before they formulated the HVO requests. The document that the Prosecution refers to is P1162. It is a report from General Siljeg, dated the 16th of January and addressed to the Main Staff, and the document says that a meeting was held and that Praljak sent a message that they would be overrun. General Praljak stated his view of the allegation from this document on the following page of the transcript, 43698, where he said that he did not address such words, nor were instructions for Siljeg formulated in this way. If you have a look at document P1174, page 1, paragraph 2, it is a document originating from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it is never mentioned in it that the message was that they would be overwhelmed. The document discusses in detail the HVO requests, and there is not a single word that would indicate that they received a threat. Page 2 of this document says the following: "In a contrary case, we shall not bear any responsibility for the consequences that may follow from the refusal of this request, which is intended to ease the tensions and the conflict and impose public law and order in the area where there is unrest." Document P1236 from Hadzihasanovic also does not mention any threat from the HVO that they would be overwhelmed. It is certain that this would be included if it had ever been expressed. In the oral presentation, the Prosecutor referred to document P1163, page 3, indicating that General Praljak was in Mostar before he came to Prozor, and that he issued an order to Miro Andric. The Prosecutor found his conclusion on the fact that a general is mentioned in the text of this document. However, the general's name is not mentioned. But, in any case, the Prosecution concludes that the general is Slobodan Praljak and that he was the one who issued the order in Mostar because General Petkovic was in Geneva. However, on the 15th and 16th of January, 1993, General Petkovic was not in Geneva. There is a series of documents which testify to that. I'm not going to enumerate them all, but 2D00471 is one that I will mention. It is the minutes on the reception of high officials of UNPROFOR to the Main Staff Command on the 16th of January, 1993, at 1500 hours, and one of those present was Milivoj Petkovic. So the Prosecution erroneously refers to this document so that the Trial Chamber would also draw a wrong conclusion from it. With regard to Gornji Vakuf, I just want to note as well that conflicts broke out before the 15th of January, 1993, so that referring to the decision on re-subordination as a trigger of conflict is unfounded, because the conflicts broke out on the 11th of January, before the decision on the re-subordination was made. And the goal of this decision was, as you will see from the documents, i.e., the presidential transcripts, to ease tensions and to end the conflict. So quite the contrary from what the Prosecution claims. And while we are still dealing with Gornji Vakuf, I also want to note what the Prosecution did in footnote 1559, in which they base their claim on a note of Witness Agic, which is page of transcript 9479, and it was not possible to do this; namely, the Prosecution should not have presented this transcript because this was the cross-examination of General Praljak. And the quoted text was the examination of Witness Agic when he examined General Praljak, and this also should not have been allowed. Therefore, what General Praljak answered to the witness, when replying to the question which he was asked, and General Praljak was the one who was doing the examination, this is something that cannot be taken as evidence. General Praljak never denied that he was present in Mostar on the 16th of January --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that he arrived in Prozor on the 16th of January. In paragraph 720 through 728, the Prosecution claims that Praljak commanded and was involved in military operations in which crimes were committed against Muslims in order to achieve the goals of a joint criminal enterprise. It is not contested that General Praljak issued orders. That was his main and principal task as the commander of the Main Staff. He did issue orders to HVO units, including those to participate in military operations. That was also his task. The orders which General Praljak issued were issued during a violent offensive launched by the Army of BiH. And throughout the trial the Prosecution did not present a single order of General Praljak which implied offensive operations or the taking of territories where the HVO had not been before such military actions. Throughout the period since June 1993 onwards, the HVO was defending itself from a violent attack. The Prosecution does not accept that, but the Trial Chamber cannot disregard it. The Prosecutor neither presented evidence nor pointed to any to confirm the allegation that crimes were committed by persons subordinated to Praljak. The case file contains testimonies by Prosecution witnesses who described those who ill-treated them as wearing both military uniforms and civilian clothes. We know that at the time, everybody wore uniforms, everybody and their uncle. They may have been soldiers in the HVO or the BiH Army, or they may have been civilians. I'm now pointing to document 3D03205, which is a statement by Witness 1D-AA, who spoke about those people who ill-treated other people in Mostar. I'm also pointing to Witness BN's testimony, which confirms that those persons wore civilian clothes. The Prosecution did not prove that crimes were committed by individuals subordinated to General Praljak, nor that General Praljak knew that crimes had been committed. It was the Prosecutor's duty to establish a link between every crime that General Praljak is charged with, and a soldier who allegedly committed it. He was not supposed to leave any possibility that those were civilians or members of another unit which was not subordinated to General Praljak. Conclusions based on indicia, if there is an alternative possibility, cannot serve as grounds for conviction here, because the circle of indicia has not been closed. Document P4399: I'm highlighting this document because the Prosecutor refers to it. What I'm saying about the document, however, is this: When Praljak arrived back from Prozor, order was restored, the situation was improved, and Praljak inspected the front-lines there. The Prosecutor, in order to show that General Praljak's orders caused the commission of crimes, refers to document P5365, which is a report on HVO successes in the course of the Muslim offensive in the month of September. However, the Prosecutor ignores the fact that that, indeed, was a Muslim offensive which had started on the 14th of September. He just gingerly points out that the situation in Rastani in September is not in the indictment; therefore, he could not refer to that situation either in the final brief or in the final argument because that situation goes beyond the scope of the temporal scope of the indictment. In paragraph 721, the Prosecutor refers to a number of documents in order to confirm the allegations. However, documents referred to in this paragraph fail to prove that General Praljak issued an order for crimes to be committed, nor does it prove that they were, indeed, committed. In order to indict General Praljak, and particularly in order to convict him, the Prosecutor was supposed to collect and then present direct proof that showed that: A, Praljak issued orders that crimes were committed by members of units subordinated directly to General Praljak; that he was informed about the crimes; and that he didn't do anything within his powers to punish those crimes. I would like to point out for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that paragraph 721 of the Prosecutor's final brief refers to Vakuf in 1993, again beyond the territorial scope of the indictment. That's why I will not belabour the point. In proving his case about the crimes committed by Praljak, in paragraph 72, the Prosecutor refers to the developments in Rastani. The Prosecutor states that crimes were committed. However, he does not establish any link between the crimes and General Praljak. The fact that Praljak appointed Stamper as commander of the Rastani front-line does not link the former with any crimes as a fact. The Prosecutor did not show any proof that Praljak received any report about the crimes in Rastani before the operation was launched on the 23rd of August, 1993 -- or, rather, during the operation on the 23rd of August, 1993. I have just been alerted to the time. It seems to be the time for our next break, or maybe not. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has been nearly one hour and thirty minutes, but we could go for another ten minutes until 12.30 or we can break now, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I can continue. I believe that General Praljak had -- or, rather, no, okay, I'll go on. The Prosecutor refers to document P4719 in his footnote 1663, and it says that General Praljak issued an order about the organisation of command system and attacks and defence activities in South-East Herzegovina Zone of Responsibility; and, furthermore, he quotes a document that proves that that order was, indeed, implemented. In a war, every order issued by a commander is meant to be executed, and that cannot constitute an element of any crime. If the Prosecutor accepted evidence on file, if the Prosecutor accepted the fact that the HVO waged a war against the BiH Army and not against the entire Muslim population, he would not claim what he did in his final brief. The Prosecutor was supposed to offer evidence to the effect that the HVO attacked the entire Muslim population. The Prosecutor did not point to any piece of evidence that would establish a link between General Praljak and any crime. He doesn't show that he may be charged with a failure to punish perpetrators within the scope of his powers. The Prosecutor has to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Praljak commanded his subordinates, that he issued orders to them to attack civilian population, that he provided his subordinates with instructions to commit crimes, that he approved crimes, and when he learned of the crimes, that he did everything possible to cover them up. Proof based on indicia can be taken into account only in a case when only one reasonable conclusion may be drawn from them, and that was -- that should be that General Praljak approved crimes and condoned crimes. I'm certain and I claim that the Trial Chamber cannot draw such inferences from the evidence in the case. The Prosecutor did not show a single piece of evidence that Praljak ever received a SIS report. As this was an organisation that was tasked with monitoring the conduct of HVO soldiers, such reports were never submitted or sent to the Main Staff of the HVO. The chief of staff does not engage in crime investigations, he does not interview witnesses, he doesn't file criminal reports, he doesn't issue indictments, he does not issue convictions. Only under those conditions could General Praljak discipline or sentence those who perpetrated crimes. When we're talking about the model of General Praljak's behaviour, and when we talk about his authority to call people to task, let's remind ourselves, he was not a prosecutor, he was not a judge; he could only discipline soldiers. We are referring to documents P3829, P4260, P5530, 3D3316, P8889 -- P8889, P7035, P2860, P5621. Due to the brevity of time at my disposal, I'm going to skip the part dealing with Humanitarian Law, because I believe that there is so much evidence on this case file testifying to the attempts undertaken by General Praljak to instruct his soldiers about the Humanitarian Law and provisions regarding the soldierly conduct. I will skip all that, and I will go straight to paragraph 728. This is the Prosecutor's conclusion about Praljak's alleged tolerance of crimes and support of crimes. The Defence of General Praljak states that General Praljak never condoned crimes, which we have managed to demonstrate clearly during the trial. As we follow his conduct from Sunje, testified by Witness Arbutina on transcript page 45091 as well as Witness Crnkovic, transcript page 45106, 3D3679, which is a statement by Dr. Mahmoud Eid, document 3D2860, as well as 3D3361, both generated by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, issued by General Praljak, so when we follow the conduct of General Praljak with regard to the protection of Serbs in Grabovina and Capljina, we have a witness statement under 3D3666. We also have Witness Curcic's testimony during trial and his statement, 3D3759. The pages in question are 3, 5 and 8, which show the model of an established conduct towards detainees. Witness BM was released, as he stated himself, in Exhibit P5530. This is another way to establish the model of behaviour which calls for discipline. The lack of discipline is punished, there is a ban on looting, ill-treatment, and there is an instruction on how to care for civilians. The Prosecution did not provide any proof that soldiers subordinate to General Praljak burned Muslim houses, that they stole their property, that they illegally detained Muslims and terrorised them, and, finally, deported them. The Prosecutor failed to prove that Praljak tolerated any such behaviour, if there was any, or that he was ever informed of any such conduct. Your Honours, I've just been told that the time has come for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now time to have a break. You have had three hours and thirty minutes. We will have a break of 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In paragraph 730, the Prosecutor quotes the alleged allegation from document P8765 and says that a subordinate reported about Praljak's command style. That subordinate said this: "General Praljak at the time said that Croats had to learn how to hate Muslims because hatred is a precondition for success in war." This is incorrect, this is misinterpretation. The text quoted by the Prosecutor is actually a journalist's text. It is not a text of any soldier that was subordinated to General Praljak. A question may be asked here: Why would General Praljak change his position and his conduct in 1993? His conduct throughout all that time was this: Crimes cannot be pardoned, crimes have to be punished; however, he could not react if he didn't know about any crimes committed. Paragraph 732 refers to a document, document P5530. The Prosecutor wants to demonstrate that the state of lawlessness reigned supreme in HVO units. We heard about this document during trial, and this document is a report of a unit which was returning from Vakuf back to the Republic of Croatia, after having spent a lot of time in the Vakuf theatre of war. They were on their way back to Croatia, yes, just like I said it. They were Croatian volunteers. The report in question says: "Our unit was charged with having looted houses in the Uskoplje front-line. We were stopped at the toll booth, allegedly pursuant to General Praljak's order. The military police inspected us, and the following appliances were found: A freezer, a fridge, an electric stove and a TV set. Those appliances were seized from those on whom they were found." This document shows that General Praljak, despite the fact that those troops had spent a long time on the front-line, he still did not tolerate looting, he did not tolerate plunder. As soon as he learned that things like that may have happened, he reacted immediately. When we speak about General Praljak's conduct and his attitude towards crime, we can quote 3D3316. This document was issued on the 1st of October, 1992. This is information about the crimes committed regularly by members of the Croatian Army. Pre-emptive action has to be based on the rule of law. Nobody, either former or present members of the Croatian Army can break the law unpunished. Nobody has acquired a possibility to be pardoned for a crime committed. Citizens' property, state property, and enemy property are protected by law. That's page 8 of the document. No one Croatian soldier can expect a crime to be forgiven to him or that criminal proceedings will not be launched. This document shows General Praljak's attitude toward crime and toward intolerable behaviour. However, General Praljak couldn't try soldiers, he couldn't press charges, nor could he convict or acquit them. There were other bodies in charge of that. I want to show that General Praljak said several times that knowing that due to the use of military police in combat activity, he will not be able to react immediately to intolerable behaviour because those responsible for crime could only later be called to responsibility, that this is true, that it was possible to hold responsible those -- hold accountable those responsible for crimes shown by the following documents: 1D2577, Operation Spider. It says that persons were deprived of liberty, who were suspected of that, in 1993 and 1994, in the area of Rama municipality, they committed crimes. The document is from 1994, document 1D1252, information about the perpetrators of crimes. Crimes are mentioned that were committed in June 1993, in September 1993, in August 1993, in November 1993, and the evidence we have led which was admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber shows that a crime was not condoned and were not part of a plan at any time. In paragraph 751, the Prosecution say that Praljak was familiar with the expulsion of Muslims. They base their claim on Witness E's testimony. However, the contents of General Praljak's speech on the transcript page cited by the Prosecution cannot be evidence because that was not testimony under oath. It was the Prosecution that insisted that General Praljak's speeches should not be admitted as evidence. Paragraph 753: On 24 September 1993, Praljak spoke to the fighters of HR-HB and spoke about the situation in the Mostar theatre and the HVO victories at Rastani and elsewhere. He was encouraging the HVO soldiers to continue their -- continue with victories. According to the Prosecution, the situation is as follows: Praljak is attacking, and he is being successful; however, for that he needs another side. In our trial brief, under the heading "BH Army," we showed documents until October 1993 which speak about the offensive of the BH Army. When this document that the Prosecution cites was drafted, Doljani had already happened on the 27th of July, 1993; Grabovica, too, 8 September 1993; Uzdol, 14 September; and the forcefulness of the offensive was recorded in the documents of the UNPROFOR unit which was in the area of Mostar and Jablanica as well as south of Mostar. If the HVO was able to slow down the BH Army offensive, clearly, the soldiers had to be informed. They had -- it was necessary to instill optimism in them and hope that the Croats will not be expelled from the areas where they lived. It was necessary to make public the fact that the HVO is being successful in slowing down or stopping the Muslim offensive, and the Prosecution act as if there had never been an offensive. About the siege of Mostar, we spoke extensively about that in our final brief, dealing with all allegations of the Prosecution; water, electricity, shelling, sniping, leaving Mostar by way of Bijela Bridge. So that for reasons of time, although I would have much to comment about that, I will move on to paragraph 761, "Convoys." I claim that the allegations made in this paragraph are refuted by evidence. It is not recorded anywhere, nor was it established during the trial, that Praljak was obstructing the convoys. Quite the contrary, when I say that, I do not have just in mind the convoy which was stopped in Citluk when General Praljak boarded an APC, and with his presence of mind when no one else managed to do that, those who were supposed to do it made it possible for this convoy to pass through to Eastern Mostar. I'm talking, rather, about all convoys which were headed to Central Bosnia and were meant to bring supplies to Muslims in Zenica throughout 1993. Document 3D00921 talks about this. The list of convoys of the 1st of June, 1993, up until the 10th of December, 1993, is to be found there. So throughout the time during which General Praljak was the commander but also before and after that time, the convoys were passing through. Of course, when the offensive of the Army of BiH was in full swing in the area of the South-Eastern Herzegovina Operation Zone when movement was dangerous, international representatives or organisations decided themselves that they would rather not pass through with their convoys. This was not prohibited by the HVO. The very same international representatives, however, did not do anything to stop the attacks launched by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Document P5926 is the protocol about the transit of humanitarian convoys, dated the 17th of October, 1993. What follows from it is that the Main Staff was not in charge of allowing the transit of the convoys. Therefore, General Praljak cannot be taken to account for the convoys, but he did allow convoys to pass through. He never prohibited a single one from transiting. Document P4027 is the Makarska Agreement about the free passage of humanitarian convoys. No one from the Main Staff was present, because the Main Staff was not responsible. The Prosecution failed to show that General Praljak obstructed convoys, and we have shown that when those responsible did not manage to secure a convoy that would go to Eastern Mostar, General Praljak did this. In paragraph 767 and 768, the Prosecution claims that General Praljak expressed his vision during the cross-examination and agreed that he advocated the separateness of peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But what crime is that, to advocate the autonomy of a constituent people in Bosnia and Herzegovina? The autonomy would not be the only case in the world where there would be an autonomous unit within a given country. Praljak never mentioned the separation of areas where Croats had lived since time immemorial, their separation from Bosnia-Herzegovina. What he did advocate was the autonomy of the Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina so that they could achieve their full constituent nation's rights. Which element of any crime defined in the Statute is a political thought, a wish, or a proposal of a political order? For such a wish to become an element of criminal responsibility of General Praljak, the Prosecution would have to prove that the events developed in such a way that this wish was achieved by force. However, the evidence shows the contrary. In paragraph 770, the Prosecution claims that Praljak advocated expulsion of Muslims in order to secure a majority Croatian population in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and refers to document P00524, which is one of the presidential transcripts. General Praljak did not advocate the expulsion of Muslims. He talked about people who were expelled by Serbs and who had come to Travnik. That resulted in a change of the ethnic composition. If they were to remain in Travnik, these people who had been expelled and who had been expelled by the VRS and the JNA, then the ethnic cleansing carried out by the VRS would be awarded. What the influx of refugees to Central Bosnia meant is also recorded by Margaret Thatcher in her book, and the relevant passage is under 3D2642. It is page 169. The burden of taking care of so many people, in particular, in Croatia and Bosnia, was unsupportable. The waves of refugees created instability, and that was their purpose. The arrival of thousands of Muslim refugees to Central Bosnia which disrupted the ethnic balance between the Muslims and the Croats is an important factor which contributed to the open war which broke out between the two sides in March 1993. 3D02637. Schrader also confirms that refugees were the cause of conflict. The Defence explained its arguments in relation to Prozor in detail in the final brief. We just want to point out here that the Trial Chamber does not have any evidence that could confirm the Prosecution thesis that General Praljak was aware of the crimes and condoned them. Quite the contrary, he punished them, which we have shown. As in its final brief and oral arguments, the Prosecution repeated that during his testimony, General Praljak said that he wanted victory, the Defence wants to refer to the transcript, and the reference is to page 40985 through 40986 on the 2nd of June, 2009: "At the time, it was important for me not to loose Gornji Vakuf or Rama. Bugojno was already lost. I did not want to lose Vakuf and everything else. The forces that were attacking us, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were about to clean everything all the way to the Croatian border. I'm not an occupier in that part." General Praljak never said that he had to win the war. He said that he must not lose the war and must not lose the areas populated by the Croats. General Praljak came at the time when the Muslim offensive was in full swing. He was at the front all the time. He had to deal with thousands upon thousands of Croatians who had left Konjic, Vares, Bugojno and Klis. Witnesses Skender, Curcic and Gerritsen talked about that. The Prosecution, during the trial, did not provide any evidence about direct perpetrators of the crimes and so as to have the right to claim that they were directly connected with General Praljak. In paragraph 785, the Prosecutor quotes the position of Judge Trechsel in order to support its own claims, and says that the Judge wanted to confirm this attitude: "No, I just note that you confirmed that your policy and your idea is if there is a murder and a victim, you remove the victim, instead of containing the murderer." For General Praljak to approve a forcible movement of a population, he should have known about it in real time. The Prosecutor had to produce at least one piece of evidence which shows that Praljak either ordered or was informed about that in real time. That would be the only way to prove that Praljak knew. The Prosecutor cannot refer to an interview given after the war about the knowledge acquired after the war. Praljak, himself, explained that between the two evils, a lesser -- the lesser evil was chosen. Lives are what matters the most, after all, and we shouldn't forget that at the time the HR-HB was faced with 50.000 refugees from Central Bosnia who arrived there not only because they wanted to be in Herzegovina, not because they were scared by any propaganda, not because they fulfilled somebody's political goals; they arrived because they wanted to save their own lives. Those people were not criminals. Only if they had been could this allegation referred to by Judge Trechsel in his remark be used as proof. Those were people on the run. They were running from the ABiH offensive after the fall of their cities, and they fled to an area where they felt safer. In a situation when there was sabotage and terrorist groups in the Dubrava Valley, when there was combat going on, and when everybody fully expected that the ABiH will continue advancing along the Neretva Valley, with the presence of a large number of frustrated, wounded, and embittered people, General Praljak, after the war, after the developments, once he was fully familiar with the reasons for the resettlement of Muslims, he said that it had been a good move because it meant that lives were saved. With regard to document P9470, I would like to point to the Trial Chamber that the piece of evidence presented in that evidence as paragraph -- as page 2 was already admitted into evidence as IC01076. When the document is evaluated, please take into account IC01076. The Prosecutor failed to show a single piece of evidence pointing to the Main Staff or General Praljak having anything to do with the detention centres. Document P7064 that the Prosecutor refers to is Biskic's report about the conditions of accommodation in detention facilities, and that document doesn't show that anything about the detention centres was under the authority of the Main Staff of the HVO. Document P7124, and the previous one was 7064, the second document, 7124, page 6, dated December 1993, not a single member of the Main Staff attended a meeting, and the list on the first page gives the names of all the detainees. This is the authorisation of Boban's order about the dismantling of all detention centres. All those that had anything to do with detention centres were there; the Ministry of Defence, the SIS Administration head, the military police, the heads of detention centres in Ljubuski, Heliodrom, Gabela, the Ministry of the Interior, the military prosecutors and judges. Nobody in the Main Staff was informed or invited to the meeting. In paragraph 813, the Prosecutor speaks about sniping, and he says that the snipers were under General Praljak's authority, and that he was well aware of the sniping activities, and that's why all the victims are down to the HVO, and Praljak is made responsible for the victims. However, the Chamber did not see any evidence to the effect that the victims were, indeed, hit by the HVO soldiers, and that snipers were only exclusively in the hands of the HVO; and that, as such, they were the only ones who could open fire on the positions of those individuals who had been hit by sniper fire. It had to be demonstrated that only an exclusively -- position in the HVO control of the western part of Mostar was the only possible position from which those victims could be either wounded or killed. The Prosecutor claims that Praljak cross-examined quite unsuccessful, without any successful argument, about the fact that snipers were under HVO command. Before the end of my final argument, I would like to point to the document P4822. This is Mazowiecki's report that the Prosecutor referred to on several occasions in his final argument. And I would like to say that it arises from that report that the constant sniping from the government position, and so far we've seen that the government or the BiH Army was positioned on the east bank of the river, and where their fire was aimed, and we could see that people in Brijeg Hospital were visited by Mazowiecki and his crew, it arises from this document that both the east and west sides of the Mostar lacked water, and it stems from that document that Mostar was destroyed already in 1992, or mostly in 1992, which is clearly demonstrated by document 1D1415. I've been informed that my time is up. Isn't it? Just a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I was warned that my time was up and that I had to provide for the half hour for the general, but I have just been -- received corrected information that I still have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had four hours until now. If General Praljak takes the floor, he will take the floor on Monday, because we must stop at a quarter to 2:00.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not done. I just thought that my time was up and I had to stop. But if I can deal with another few paragraphs of the Prosecution brief, I'll do that with great pleasure. So I broke off when I was speaking about the snipers. In paragraph 814, the Prosecution speaks about Praljak's knowledge about snipers in Mostar. However, the documents they cite actually say -- speak to the contrary. I have already mentioned P4822. With regard to document P10047, that's a statement of which I'm not sure at the moment whether it's confidential, so I won't state the name. The Prosecution refers to paragraphs 47, 44 and 46. I must point out to the Trial Chamber that paragraph 44 of the statement is not in evidence, so that the Trial Chamber cannot base its decision on that. About General Praljak's knowledge about the snipers, it was the Prosecution's duty to prove that they were HVO snipers and that the victims were hit by their snipers. Then they had to prove that General Praljak knew of the snipers, and, based on that, draw such conclusions. As it is, it all rests on the Prosecution's allegations, without any evidence. In our final brief, we analysed each and every sniping incident and all the victims hit by snipers, and showed that no one victim could have been hit from HVO positions. With regard to the destruction of Mostar and what it looked like, I would like to refer to document 1D01415. That is the Mostar morning of 11 June 1992. That's a document issued by the 1st Mostar Independent Battalion, and it's a publication of the BH Army, in which it says: "June 92: Raving pyromaniacs have reduced Luka, Donja Mahala, Main Street and Fejic Street, a large part of Cernica and Semovac, Cim and Ilici to cinders. The beastly Greater Serbian and Greater Montenegrin thirst for blood, the criminal instinct for looting and killing, the delirious concept of creating a twilight zone on the banks of the Neretva to draw ethnic borders in -- imagined in the darkest depths of a disturbed mind have levelled a cultural and historical heritage which was four centuries' old, devastated Muslim and Catholic shrines, ploughed over graves, and expelled people from their centuries-old homes." So that Mostar was actually destroyed in 1992, and not in 1993, as claimed by the Prosecution witnesses and as alleged by the Prosecution in their final brief. This was written by Bosniaks in 1992, and I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to take this into consideration. In paragraph 820, the Prosecution says American Ambassador Peter Galbraith has summed up his opinion about Praljak's responsibility not only about the shelling and destruction of Eastern Mostar, but also concerning all of his crimes. That included the JCE. This is a general assessment of Ambassador Galbraith. Of course, it is his right to put forward arbitrary assessments and unconfirmed allegations, but it is up to the Trial Chamber to reach the decision only based on evidence led by both sides, both parties to the proceedings. In paragraphs 839 through 846, the Prosecution claim that Praljak's testimony, with which he wanted to help himself, is not trustworthy. Although Mr. Praljak's testimony is not trustworthy, the final brief is full of lines from his testimony, and the allegations in 57 paragraphs actually cite his testimony. The Prosecution says when Praljak did not lie, then he avoided answering. About the lies: Praljak, in his testimony, showed a map of Gornji Vakuf which did not show the HVO artillery positions on Mount Makljen. By doing so, he failed to give important information to the Trial Chamber, and he showed them a wrong map that showed only BH Army positions. However, the positions of the HVO artillery with regard to the events in Vakuf was irrelevant, which follows from Tokic's testimony. Praljak drew a map showing the BH Army positions. By drawing the map, Praljak showed the BH Army positions. Because of the Prosecutor's insisting that the HVO attacked the Muslim population, showing a map where the BH Army positions had as its goal to show that there were BH Army forces, and that this wasn't an attack on the Muslim population. According to the testimony of Witness Tokic, the artillery on Makljen couldn't target the town because it was out of reach. P1162: Siljeg's report, "Our Forces." In the description of the activities, it was not mentioned that from the area of Makljen, fire was opened upon Gornji Vakuf/Uskoplje, but rather on Crni Vrh and Voljevac, BH Army positions. The report points out the BH Army strongholds south of the town of Gornji Vakuf; namely, Uzice, Dusa, Mount Mackovac, and the strengthened lines at Podovi. The Prosecution's allegations that only civilians were present at Uzice and Dusa, and that, thus, the Muslim population was attacked, is unfounded. In the direct examination, Praljak said that Eastern Mostar did not complain to international representatives about shortage of water. In the cross-examination, he was faced with a document in which he was informed about the shortage of water in Eastern Mostar. This is a misinterpretation, and actually the Prosecution was asking -- was asking leading questions. The following lie: When answering Judge Antonetti's questions about his possible conversations with Tudjman while he was the chief of the Main Staff, Praljak lied, because on cross he was faced with evidence showing that on the 15th of September, 1993, he was in Tudjman's office. Praljak said that he never spoke with Tudjman about the way military operations were conducted, and he also said that he didn't receive orders either from Tudjman or even Boban when he came to the planning of defence and commanding operations. In other words, General Praljak did not lie, whereas the Prosecution erroneously interpreted the contents of the documents and minutes. The following lie: Praljak lied when he said that the Tudjman and Milosevic agreement was created in 1993, when pressure had to be put on Croats. He was faced with Filipovic's interview, of whom he said that he was an honourable Muslim. In the month of June 1991, he spoke about the Tudjman-Milosevic agreement. Praljak said that the rumours of a division of Bosnia between Tudjman and Milosevic started circulating around Croatia already in 1993 anyway. Alija Izetbegovic was well aware of the meeting between Tudjman and Milosevic. He was even aware of the alleged topic of the conversation, which is corroborated by document 3D00295. The document is Alija Izetbegovic's letter to Dr. Tudjman, dated 24 March 1991. And in the letter, it says: "I am convinced, Mr. President, and I have certain proof and information to that effect, that he," "He" with a capital letter and underlined, "in bilateral talks, will offer you certain partial solutions which, to a certain extent, would be to the expense of Muslims and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Please turn any such offer down, because you know that those offers accepted would lead to chaos ...," and so on and so forth. However, at that time the rumours about Karadjordjevo did not blow out of proportions, as they did in 1994. It became particularly absurd when the JNA launched an all-out attack on the Republic of Croatia. Then the rumours quieted down. In 1994, when Manolic and Mesic left the HDZ and established their own party and were preparing for a take-over, the story about Karadjordjevo became topical again because it was necessary to destabilise the Republic of Croatia and Dr. Franjo Tudjman. Therefore, General Praljak didn't lie. Another lie: Praljak denied knowledge about the tank on Stotina. Under oath, Praljak lied that he didn't know about the tank in Stotina, whereas his book shows the position of the tank on Stotina. The Prosecutor completely ignores the fact that General Praljak said that at the relevant time in November 1993, he did not know that there was a tank on Stotina. Only subsequently, when he investigated the circumstances of the destruction of the Old Bridge was he able to establish that there was a tank on Stotina; and then, for the purpose of truthfully representing all the circumstances surrounding the destruction of the Old Bridge in a book, which was the result of all that evidence collected, he did show the position of the tank on Stotina. It is one thing to know something in November 1993 and an entirely different thing to have subsequent information as a result of the collection of data. This can certainly not be qualified as a lie. The Defence claims that the OTP failed to prove that General Praljak did any violations of the law as a commander. They didn't prove that Slobodan Praljak committed a great breach of his duties, that any such possible breach may have been serious, willful and wanton. Therefore, General Praljak cannot be held responsible pursuant to 7/3. Only the most serious deviations from the duties of a commander constitute criminal liability, and this Trial Chamber has been deprived of any proof that would demonstrate that General Praljak behaved in a criminal way pursuant to 7/3. For all those reasons, General Praljak's Defence believes that this Trial Chamber [as interpreted] should be acquitted of all charges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That General Praljak should be acquitted of all charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is soon going to be time to adjourn. We'll resume on Monday with General Praljak. Until then, I wish you all a good evening. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
